video_title: Ethereum’s Staking Yield Could Go to Zero
gist: Bankless weekly rollup: Ryan and David dissect the new tapered-issuance-burn EIP that would zero out ETH staking rewards above 50% stake (cutting today's base yield from ~2.6% to ~1.2%), and conclude it is dead on arrival because every DeFi builder opposes it. They also read the S&P's V-shaped recovery to all-time highs after Aschbrenner's forced liquidation as proof the AI trade isn't done, argue Bitcoin can't bottom until AI capitulates, and unpack the Coldcard weak-entropy exploit that drained ~$130M from supposedly offline hardware wallets.

themes.theme: AI-trade V-recovery and the Aschbrenner liquidation

insights.claim: The S&P 500 round-tripped a 5-6% July drawdown in days, ripping roughly 3% in a single weekly candle from about 7,500 to nearly 7,800 and printing an all-time high in the first week of August, while the Nasdaq (down about 10% in July) has not yet reclaimed its high.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The index-level all-time high masks a still-incomplete Nasdaq recovery, so relative Nasdaq-vs-S&P strength is the cleaner tell on whether the AI trade has fully re-risked.
insights.quote: the weekly candle in the S&P is a 3% candle that brought it from 7,500 all the way up to the tippy top almost 7,800

insights.claim: David attributes the V-shaped equity recovery to Leopold Aschbrenner's fund being force-liquidated at the exact low with Citadel stepping in to absorb the positions, which then gave the market the confidence to buy.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: If a single levered forced seller was the marginal supply, the flush is now cleared and dip-buying AI exposure carries less overhang risk than the drawdown implied.
insights.quote: this was all on the backs of uh Leopold from uh a situation awareness getting liquidated right at the bottom

insights.claim: Aschbrenner's fund shrank from a $20-30 billion peak to roughly $8-10 billion (mostly private positions after public ones were liquidated) and was down 67% in July, yet is still up about 80% on the year.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: The fund survived rather than died, so there is no Tiger-style multi-quarter unwind of AI positions still to come from this holder.
insights.quote: The The fund went from 20 to 30 billion dollar peak to about 8 to 10 billion remaining.

insights.claim: Aschbrenner was reported to be running roughly 400% leverage, which the hosts frame as a risk-management failure rather than a thesis failure, since he had to call Ken Griffin to take the bags mid-liquidation.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Leverage, not the AI thesis, was what broke, which is why the underlying assets recovered immediately after the position was cleared.
insights.quote: He was reported to be on 400% leverage

insights.claim: The speed of the equity recovery is read as market confirmation that participants believe the AI trade is not over and are willing to re-enter immediately after a violent liquidation.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Positioning stays crowded in AI, which caps rotation into crypto and other laggards until that consensus cracks.
insights.quote: It does seem like confirmation that at least the market thinks the game is not over for AI and the AI trade continues.

themes.theme: Bitcoin cycle read and time-based capitulation

insights.claim: Ryan argues crypto cannot fully bottom until the AI trade is over and the market acknowledges it, because investors remain disproportionately allocated to AI and Nasdaq rather than rotating back into crypto.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Treat AI-trade exhaustion as the leading indicator for crypto's cycle low rather than crypto-native metrics.
insights.quote: the AI trade might have to die in order for crypto to live

insights.claim: David sees no remaining forced sellers of Bitcoin - even Saylor selling and price rising - so the next leg down would have to come from opportunity-cost sellers rotating into outperforming AI names.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Watch relative performance versus semis and memory names, not leverage or liquidation data, for the mechanism that finally exhausts Bitcoin holders.
insights.quote: So like who's going to be the forced seller? The answer is like no one.

insights.claim: David introduces time-based capitulation as the operative concept: six to nine more months of the AI trade running could exhaust Bitcoin holders who sell out of boredom and opportunity cost rather than margin calls.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Sets a rough six-to-nine month clock on the crypto bottom and argues against buying an early Bitcoin capitulation signal.
insights.quote: you could see the AI trade running for six more months, nine more months, and then the time based capitulation of Bitcoin holders

insights.claim: Memory stocks are cited as up 5,000%, illustrating the scale of relative-performance pain that would drive Bitcoin holders to rotate.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The rotation risk is quantified by an extreme performance spread, meaning the pain trade is holding flat crypto against parabolic semis.
insights.quote: even though memory stocks have gone up 5,000%

insights.claim: Bitcoin has been riding its 200-week moving average around $62,000-$64,000 for roughly six weeks since mid-June, trading at about $64,500 at the time of recording.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The 200-week MA near $64k is the operative line in the sand; a decisive break below it changes the cycle read.
insights.quote: We are we have been riding the 200-week moving average since um the middle of June

insights.claim: Historically Bitcoin only spent an extended period (roughly 40 days or more) below the 200-week moving average after the 3AC, Luna and FTX contagion, whereas recent breaks have lasted under a week.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Sustained time below the 200-week MA has historically required a solvency crisis, so brief dips beneath it are not yet regime change.

insights.claim: David's chart-based view is that the current cycle looks roughly 85% complete from the $130,000 high, implying a bit more downside followed by a year-and-a-half U-shaped bear market.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Implies patience over accumulation urgency: the shape argues for a long basing period rather than a fast V in crypto.
insights.quote: the visual shape of the chart looks 85% complete, but not 100%

insights.claim: The hosts disagree on Bitcoin-Nasdaq correlation: Ryan says Bitcoin is up on the week because Nasdaq is up and correlation is elevated, while David counters that the two charts simply do not look alike.
insights.speaker: Ryan and David
insights.so_what: Short-window correlation may be misleading traders into using Nasdaq as a Bitcoin proxy when the cycle shapes have diverged.
insights.quote: if you look at the Nasdaq chart and the Bitcoin chart, those are just different looking charts

themes.theme: Saylor de-rated as Bitcoin's marginal pricer

insights.claim: Strategy sold 1,638 Bitcoin worth about $105 million and Bitcoin rose from $62,000 to $63,500 on the week, versus the first sale of just 32 Bitcoin that collapsed the price by roughly $18,000.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The market has fully priced Strategy's forward selling, so future disclosed sales are no longer a tradable short catalyst.
insights.quote: MicroStrategy Strategy announced that it sold 1,638 Bitcoin worth 105 million, and Bitcoin jumps from 62,000 to 63 and 1/2 thousand dollars

insights.claim: David is bullish on the news specifically because it removes Michael Saylor as a key-man risk and marginal pricer of Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Reframes Strategy's selling as a structural de-risking of Bitcoin rather than a bearish supply event.
insights.quote: Michael Saylor needs to be removed from the market as a key man risk to Bitcoin price

insights.claim: The market's expectation is a graceful, non-cascading unwind of Strategy's leverage: mint MSTR shares whenever a premium exists and sell Bitcoin to pay preferred shareholders, which is good for Bitcoin holders but not necessarily for MSTR holders.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Separates the trades: the Bitcoin overhang is known and orderly, while equity and preferred holders absorb the dilution and unwind cost.
insights.quote: he's going to sell Bitcoin in order to pay preferred share owners

insights.claim: Strategy's STRC preferred is back above $90, up about 30% from June lows around $71, which the hosts read as a much healthier capital structure.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: STRC's recovery from $71 is the market's live solvency gauge on Strategy's preferred stack and was a high-return entry point at the lows.
insights.quote: I notice STRC is back up above 90.

themes.theme: Tapered issuance burn: how the ETH proposal actually works

insights.claim: On August 4th six Ethereum researchers including Justin Drake, Jerome Dechechere, Daplion and Pintail proposed a tapered issuance burn that destroys a slice of staking rewards before stakers receive them, with the burnt slice growing as the staked share of supply rises.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: A live monetary-policy proposal on the largest yield-bearing crypto asset is the single biggest swing factor for ETH staking economics.
insights.quote: what this proposal does is that Ethereum starts destroying, burning a slice of the rewards before stakers receive them

insights.claim: Under the proposal the entire staking reward is burnt once about 50% of all ETH is staked (versus roughly 33% staked today), with only about 5% of otherwise-issued rewards paid at 45% stake, shutting off the incentive to stake beyond that threshold.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Gives a hard, modelable ceiling on staking participation and therefore on future LST supply growth if it ever passes.
insights.quote: Meaning staking pays essentially nothing beyond 50% stake, and the incentive to stake more ETH basically shuts off.

insights.claim: If implemented today, the base staking yield for existing ETH stakers would drop roughly in half, from about 2.6% to about 1.2%.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: A halving of the base rate would immediately reprice LST yields, staking-ETH treasury vehicles and DeFi leverage loops built on that rate.
insights.quote: their base staking yield drops roughly in half from about 2.6% yield to 1.2% yield

insights.claim: David corrects a common misconception: absolute ETH issuance always rises as more ETH is staked, and only the rate of new issuance falls, which is why nothing today stops the staked share marching toward 100%.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The proposal's entire premise rests on this distinction; investors modeling ETH dilution off the declining rate alone are understating supply growth.
insights.quote: Issuance always goes up the more ETH gets staked. The rate of new issuance goes down as more ETH gets staked.

insights.claim: The pro case rests on Ethereum overpaying for security and on precedent, since proof-of-work issuance was cut from five ETH per block to three to two before the merge under a minimum-viable-issuance social contract.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Issuance cuts have historical precedent on Ethereum, so holders should not assume monetary policy is ossified.
insights.quote: the pro argument for tapering targeting is that Ethereum is overpaying for security

insights.claim: The second pro argument is that unbounded staking incentives erode vanilla ETH's money-ness and centralize the network on LSTs, since at 100% staked the circulating money of the Ethereum economy becomes Lido stETH or Rocket Pool rETH rather than ETH itself.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Frames LST dominance as a monetary-capture risk, analogous to an economy transacting in money-market shares instead of dollars.
insights.quote: a constraintless amount of incentive to stake ETH erodes vanilla ETH's money-ness and centralizes the network on LSTs

themes.theme: Issuance war: EF researchers versus the app layer

insights.claim: The opposition's core argument is that halving staking revenue against unchanged fixed costs prices out solo and home stakers while favoring industrial operators like Lido and Figment, accelerating the very centralization the proposal claims to fix.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: The proposal's second-order effect could increase LST and professional-operator share, the opposite of the stated intent.
insights.quote: Well, you just cut their revenue in half, but they have the same fixed costs.

insights.claim: Staking yield functions as DeFi's base rate, underpinning leveraged staking loops, LST collateral on Aave, structured products and institutional treasury allocations, so tapering it toward zero would drain ETH out of DeFi and shrink TVL.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Any serious progress on this EIP would be a direct short signal for ETH-collateralized DeFi TVL and lending-market volumes.
insights.quote: staking yield is DeFi's base rate

insights.claim: Aave founder Stani publicly opposed the proposal, arguing Ethereum's priorities should be privacy, scalability and security, and that unpredictable yield is a negative for institutional buyers and makes ETH borrowing strategies mostly unviable.
insights.speaker: David (quoting Stani)
insights.so_what: Institutional ETH yield strategies depend on predictability, so even the debate itself raises the discount rate on ETH-based structured products.
insights.quote: Ethereum should not focus on gaming, staking issuance, and cutting staking rewards. That is not the problem Ethereum needs to solve. Priorities are privacy, scalability, and security.

insights.claim: Mike Silagadze of EtherFi called the EIP disappointing on every level, citing only 48 hours' notice and arguing it reinforces critics' view that Ethereum is run by a small group of insiders.
insights.speaker: David (quoting Mike Silagadze)
insights.so_what: Process legitimacy, not just economics, is now a governance risk factor for Ethereum in the eyes of the largest LST businesses.
insights.quote: Disappointing on every level. EIP released with only 48 hours' notice. Every builder on Ethereum opposes this.

insights.claim: David treats the unanimity of ETH DeFi builders against the proposal as the most important signal, because Stani, Mike and Lido have skin in the game while researchers do not have businesses built on the ecosystem.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Skin-in-the-game alignment is a usable filter for predicting which Ethereum governance fights actually resolve.
insights.quote: the people with skin in the game are saying no

insights.claim: Ryan raises the ossification argument that every time monetary dials are moved, you prove the dials can be moved and hand Bitcoin's 21-million critique fresh ammunition, so any issuance change should require Congress-level overwhelming consensus.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Sets a bar for future ETH monetary changes that implies most such proposals will fail, supporting ETH's credibility as a store of value.
insights.quote: anytime you move the dials, you prove that the dials can be moved

insights.claim: David argues the strongest anti-argument is path dependency around large new institutional buyers: Tom Lee just bought 5% of ETH explicitly to stake it for yield, and retroactively removing that yield would be an adulteration of the social contract that could push him to sell.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Names a concrete large-holder sell catalyst tied to the EIP, making it a live tail risk for ETH price if the proposal ever advances.
insights.quote: Tom Lee just bought 5% of ETH, and his whole entire idea is that he gets to stake it and get the yield, and we're just rugging that from him.

insights.claim: David likes the proposal on technical purity but would vote no because of DeFi and institutional path dependency, suggesting that if done at all the stake target should glide from 100% down to 50% over about a decade rather than jump.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Even sympathetic insiders think timing and gradualism are disqualifying, lowering the odds of any near-term ETH yield cut.
insights.quote: I like the proposal in a vacuum, but there's too much baggage to say yes.

insights.claim: Ryan applies an Occam's test - would implementation make him more bullish or more bearish on ETH - and concludes more bearish, rejecting the proposal even in a vacuum because the benefits are vague and second-order compared with the merge's obvious payoff.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: A simple bull/bear implementation test is a usable heuristic for pricing governance proposals in any token.
insights.quote: would this make me more bullish or more bearish on ETH? And the conclusion there is more bearish.

insights.claim: Ryan puts the probability of the proposal passing at quickly approaching zero, under 5%, and predicts there will be no issuance changes given the reception it received.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: If correct, ETH holders can ignore the headline yield-to-zero risk and any price weakness on this news is noise to fade.
insights.quote: it is dead in the water at this point and I I predict there will be no issuance changes

insights.claim: Ryan reframes the failed proposal as evidence Ethereum governance works, since a proposal was published, stakeholders weighed in, rough consensus was not reached and it was shot down.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Counters the capture narrative that critics will attach to the episode, which matters for ETH's institutional credibility story.
insights.quote: No, this is what decentralization actually looks like. This is the messy process of decentralization taking place.

themes.theme: Coldcard weak-entropy exploit and the self-custody crisis

insights.claim: Roughly $130 million of Bitcoin has been drained from offline Coldcard hardware wallets, including Jonathan Goodman who lost 18.2 BTC (over C$1.6 million) from a device kept in a safety deposit box that never touched the internet.
insights.speaker: David and Ryan
insights.so_what: Air-gapping and seed-phrase hygiene did not protect holders, which resets the assumed security floor for self-custodied Bitcoin.
insights.quote: 130 million dollars total in Bitcoin being exploited from offline hardware wallets

insights.claim: The root cause was weak entropy: Coldcard shipped with a much better random number generator that was never switched on, so seed generation had a detectable pattern that let attackers use AI to shrink the search space and brute-force keys.
insights.speaker: David and Ryan
insights.so_what: The failure is a vendor implementation bug, not a protocol flaw, so due diligence on RNG implementation becomes a real custody criterion.
insights.quote: it had a a random number generator that was like much better but it was not actually switched on

insights.claim: Every private key generated on a Coldcard from roughly 2021 onward is potentially guessable, and attacks are arriving in waves as hackers fingerprint Coldcard wallet profiles, so the hosts' advice is to migrate off the device immediately.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: An identifiable cohort of vulnerable wallets means continuing drains and a steady, predictable stream of forced coin movement.
insights.quote: everyone who used a cold card cold card wallet from this time period from like, you know, 2000 it 21 and and beyond actually generated private keys that could be guessed by some attacker

insights.claim: The hosts state the flaw does not exist in the more popular Trezor and Ledger wallets, which have since emphasized how their randomness is generated.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Contains the blast radius to one vendor and suggests share shift toward Ledger, Trezor and multisig products rather than a wholesale exit from self-custody.
insights.quote: this problem does not exist in the Trezor Ledger wallets

insights.claim: David identifies AI as the common denominator across both the entropy exploit and social-engineering attacks, citing a friend who lost her browser-extension funds after three AI-faked video meetings led her to download a corrupted version of Obsidian.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Security spend and product design should assume AI-augmented attackers on both the cryptographic and human layers.
insights.quote: AI is shaking the foundations of self-custody

insights.claim: David argues offensive AI capability is currently outpacing defensive patching, producing the fewest self-custody users since 2021-2022, with some expecting migration of Bitcoin into ETFs and exchanges where these attacks are not possible.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Structurally bullish for custodial venues and spot ETFs and bearish for hardware-wallet and DeFi self-custody adoption until defenses catch up.
insights.quote: it's like the darkest days for self-custody ever

themes.theme: Uniswap's launchpad and Robinhood-chain fee economics

insights.claim: Uniswap launched pools.trade, its own native token launchpad, offering a crowd launch with a 4-hour TWAP auction that is bundle-resistant and graduates at a $10,000 fully diluted valuation or refunds participants, plus an instant bonding-curve launch, both ending in a Uniswap V4 pool with fixed 1 billion supply.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Uniswap is verticalizing into token creation, competing directly for the meme-coin issuance fee pool on Ethereum.
insights.quote: It's pump fun for Ethereum.

insights.claim: Fees collected by pools.trade are routed back into buying the launched token itself rather than being extracted from the liquidity pool, which is pitched as a structural price benefit to encourage adoption.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: A fee-to-buyback design is the differentiator Uniswap is using to pull launches away from incumbent launchpads.
insights.quote: the the fees collected by this go back into buying the token itself

insights.claim: Uniswap V3, V2 and V4 are the top three DEXs on Robinhood chain and together account for about 99% of its DEX volume.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Near-total DEX dominance on a major retail distribution chain is a durable, measurable revenue moat for Uniswap.
insights.quote: that's to combined 99% of DEX volume on Robinhood chain

insights.claim: Robinhood chain has doubled the rate at which UNI is bought back and burned - more than all other chains combined - driven by meme coin activity that represents about 50% of all meme coin activity in crypto, with UNI recently hitting an 8-to-10 month high.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete cash-flow driver for the UNI token tied to a single venue's meme coin volumes, which is both the bull case and the concentration risk.
insights.quote: the amount of Uni being bought back and burned by the protocol has doubled because of Robinhood chain

insights.claim: The hosts read Uniswap's renewed shipping cadence as a shift into founder mode driven by regulatory malaise lifting and by treasury runway forcing the organization to generate positive economics.
insights.speaker: Ryan and David
insights.so_what: A protocol pivoting from treasury-funded to revenue-driven behavior is a re-rating catalyst for its token.
insights.quote: Hayden's tweets for the last 2 months feel more like founder mode

themes.theme: Policy stall, prediction markets and new distribution rails

insights.claim: Polymarket odds on the Clarity Act collapsed from 41% two weeks ago to 28% last week to 15% now, after no cloture was filed before recess and Democrats continued holding out on the ethics issue.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: US crypto market-structure legislation is effectively off the table this year, pushing the timeline past the midterms.
insights.quote: So 2 weeks ago we were at 41% probability on Polymarket, 28% last week, now it's 15%.

insights.claim: The hosts predict the Clarity Act does not pass this year and possibly not at all, with the next real window depending on whether the incoming Congress after the midterms picks it up.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Removes a widely anticipated regulatory catalyst from 2026 crypto forecasts.
insights.quote: I think it's not going to happen this year for sure

insights.claim: The strategic workaround proposed is to stack irreversible institutional wins - once BlackRock has tokenized its assets, no future administration can credibly force an unwind - so momentum substitutes for legislation.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Institutional tokenization progress, not legislation, becomes the metric to track for durable regulatory protection.
insights.quote: once BlackRock has tokenized its assets, was like Democrat administration, are they going to tell BlackRock, Larry Fink, like, "Hey, sorry, you got to undo all of that."

insights.claim: The cost of no Clarity Act falls asymmetrically on young and future startups rather than incumbents like BlackRock, which are already protected.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Regulatory stalemate entrenches large incumbents and suppresses the early-stage crypto formation rate, a headwind for venture returns.
insights.quote: there are probably a bunch of theoretical, hypothetical startups that won't exist because clarity clarity is not a thing

insights.claim: Polymarket is seeking investment at more than a $20 billion valuation, which Ryan considers reasonable given exchange economics and take rates, versus roughly $9 billion earlier around the ICE deal talks.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Prediction-market valuations are compounding fast, and retail access via IPO or token remains the missing piece.
insights.quote: 20 billion seems about right

insights.claim: David frames the prediction-market valuation debate as sports book comp (roughly $10-30 billion) versus CME comp (roughly $100-200 billion), arguing Polymarket is still in the sports book range and far from the CME story.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit valuation ceiling test: watch for non-sports, financial-contract volume as the trigger for the CME multiple.
insights.quote: everyone in crypto wants less of the sports book comp and more of the CME comp

insights.claim: Robinhood's prediction market revenue is now twice its crypto revenue, evidence that prediction markets are a highly monetizable category attracting more competitors.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Prediction markets are already a larger revenue line than crypto at a major retail broker, which reframes the category's addressable market.
insights.quote: Robinhood's prediction market revenue is now two x's is crypto revenue

insights.claim: Cloudflare launched wallets for storing stablecoins, purchasing services and receiving funds, which David interprets as effectively a wallet for bots so AI crawlers must pay the creators whose content they scrape.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Machine-to-machine stablecoin payments for content access is a concrete first rail for agentic payments at internet scale.
insights.quote: the idea is like this is actually a wallet for bots

insights.claim: NEAR launched staking for NEAR AI where staking the NEAR token yields free confidential inference from NEAR's distributed GPU clusters, which the hosts classify as a genuine work or utility token rather than a speculative one.
insights.speaker: David and Ryan
insights.so_what: A revival of the work-token model tying token staking to a consumable AI service is a template other infra tokens may copy.
insights.quote: You stake NEAR, you get inference.

insights.claim: David argues tokenized stocks and real-world assets remain blocked by roughly 17 competing standards with no leader, which prevents perp platforms from internalizing a full perp-spot basis trade and constrains what can be built on chain.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Standards consolidation in tokenized equities is the specific unlock to watch before perp DEX volumes can step-change.
insights.quote: There's like 17 competing standards and not one of them has really taken the lead.

insights.claim: David's state-of-crypto view is that on-chain activity has cycled back to meme coins while DeFi and self-custody struggle, describing a waiting game of six to nine months of boredom and capitulation before the working use cases assert themselves.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a low-catalyst grind rather than an imminent narrative rotation, favoring patience over chasing on-chain themes.
insights.quote: Like not DeFi's not great. Like self-custody not great. Uh like it's just meme coins.
